source_text:
Credentes itaque in deum patrem omnipotentem nullam creaturam esse, quae ab omnipotente non creata sit, existimare debemus. et quia omnia per uerbum creauit, quod uerbum et ueritas dicitur et uirtus et sapientia dei multisque aliis insinuatur uocabulis qui nostrae fidei Iesus Christus dominus commendatur, liberator scilicet noster et rector filius dei — non enim uerbum illud, per quod sunt omnia condita, generare potuit nisi ille, qui per ipsum condidit omnia -
credimus etiam in Iesum Christum filium dei patris unigenitum, id est unicum, dominum nostrum. quod tamen uerbum non sicut uerba nostra debemus accipere, quae uoce atque ore prolata uerberato aere transeunt nec diutius manent quam sonant; manet enim illud uerbum incommutabiliter. nam de ipso dictum est, cum de sapientia diceretur: in se ipsa manens innouat omnia. uerbum enim patris ideo dictum est, quia per ipsum innotescit pater. sicut enim uerbis nostris id agimus, cum uerum loquimur, ut noster animus innotescat audienti et quidquid secretum in corde gerimus per signa huius modi ad cognitionem alterius proferatur: sic illa sapientia, quam deus pater genuit, quoniam per ipsam innotescit dignis animis secretissimus pater, uerbum eius \'conuenientissime nominatur.
thought_title: The Word through whom all things were made
orientation: Augustine is explaining the first article of the creed about God the Father almighty, and now moves to the second article about the Son, the Word through whom all things were made.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore believing in God the Father almighty, we ought to think that no creature exists which has not been created by the almighty. And because he created all things through the Word, which Word is also called truth and power and wisdom of God and is indicated by many other names, and is commended to our faith as Jesus Christ the Lord, namely our liberator and ruler, the Son of God — for that Word, through which all things were founded, could not have been begotten except by him who founded all things through it — we believe also in Jesus Christ, the only Son of God the Father, that is the unique one, our Lord. But we ought not to take that Word as our words, which, uttered by voice and mouth, pass through the struck air and do not remain longer than they sound; for that Word remains unchangeably. For it was said of it, when it was said of wisdom: remaining in herself she renews all things. For the Word of the Father is called so because through it the Father becomes known. For just as with our words we bring it about, when we speak the truth, that our mind becomes known to the hearer and whatever secret we carry in our heart is brought forth through signs of this kind to the knowledge of another: so that wisdom, which God the Father begot, because through it the most secret Father becomes known to worthy minds, is most fittingly named his Word.

choices.why: The verb means 'commended' or 'recommended' to faith, not 'entrusted'; the Word is presented to our faith as Jesus Christ the Lord.
The ablative absolute describes the air being struck by the voice; 'struck air' preserves the physical image of spoken words passing away.
rejected: through the air that is struck

choices.term: in se ipsa manens innouat omnia
choices.english: remaining in herself she renews all things
choices.why: The feminine 'ipsa' refers to wisdom (sapientia), and 'manens' is a present participle; the rendering keeps the participial force and the feminine subject.
rejected: while remaining in herself she renews all things
she remains in herself and renews all things

choices.why: The superlative adverb emphasizes the appropriateness of the name 'Word' for the wisdom begotten by the Father.

bible_refs.note: in se ipsa manens innouat omnia

pass_b_english: Therefore, since we believe in God the Father almighty, we must hold that no creature exists that was not created by the Almighty. And because he created all things through the Word—the Word who is also called the truth and the power and the wisdom of God, and who is commended to our faith under many other names as Jesus Christ our Lord, that is, our liberator and ruler, the Son of God—for that Word through whom all things were made could be begotten by none except the one who made all things through him—we believe also in Jesus Christ, the only Son of God the Father, that is, his unique one, our Lord.

But we must not understand that Word as we understand our own words, which are produced by voice and mouth, strike the air, and pass away, lasting no longer than their sound. That Word remains unchangeably. For it was said of him when Scripture spoke of wisdom: “Remaining in herself, she renews all things” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27). He is called the Word of the Father because through him the Father becomes known. Just as when we speak true words, we act so that our mind becomes known to the hearer, and whatever secret we carry in our heart is brought to another's knowledge through signs of this kind, so wisdom whom God the Father begot is most fittingly named his Word, because through her the most hidden Father becomes known to worthy souls.

problems.why: Active 'generare potuit' = 'could beget/generate', not passive 'could have been begotten'. Agency reversed.
problems.fix: for that Word through whom all things were made could generate nothing except by the one who made all things through him
problems.ruling: 'generare potuit' is active: 'could beget/generate'. English 'could have been begotten' reverses agency.

problems.quote: so that wisdom whom God the Father begot is most fittingly named his Word
problems.source_quote: sic illa sapientia...uerbum eius conuenientissime nominatur
problems.why: The 'sic...sicut' construction ('just as...so') is broken: 'sicut enim uerbis nostris...sic illa sapientia...nominatur'. English 'so that' introduces purpose/result, not the comparative 'so/just so'. Should be 'so that wisdom...is named'.
problems.fix: so that wisdom whom God the Father begot is most fittingly named his Word
problems.ruling: 'so that' implies purpose/result; 'sic' = 'so/just so' in comparative with 'sicut'. Misleads reader on structure.

edits.old: for that Word through whom all things were made could not have been begotten except by the one who made all things through him
edits.new: for that Word through whom all things were made could beget nothing except by the one who made all things through him

edits.old: so that wisdom whom God the Father begot is most fittingly named his Word
edits.new: so wisdom whom God the Father begot is most fittingly named his Word

fixed: Changed 'could not have been begotten' to 'could beget nothing': source 'generare potuit' is active, meaning the Word could beget/generate, not be begotten.
Changed 'so that wisdom' to 'so wisdom': source 'sic illa sapientia...nominatur' is the comparative 'so' completing 'sicut...sic', not a purpose clause.

problems.quote: for that Word through whom all things were made could beget nothing except by the one who made all things through him
problems.source_quote: non enim uerbum illud, per quod sunt omnia condita, generare potuit nisi ille, qui per ipsum condidit omnia
problems.why: Agency reversed: source says the Father alone could beget the Word, not that the Word could beget nothing.
problems.fix: for that Word through whom all things were made could be begotten by none except the one who made all things through him

fixed: Agency reversed: source 'generare potuit nisi ille' means the Word could be begotten only by the Father, not that the Word could beget nothing; corrected to 'could be begotten by none except the one who made all things through him'.

last_rejected.why: 'unicum' means 'the only one/unique one,' referring to the Son, not 'his unique one.'
last_rejected.ruling: 'unicum' as predicate nominative refers to Son; 'his unique one' is normal English rendering of 'unigenitum...unicum' construction.

last_rejected.quote: For it was said of him when Scripture spoke of wisdom
last_rejected.source_quote: nam de ipso dictum est, cum de sapientia diceretur
last_rejected.why: Source says 'when wisdom was being spoken of,' not 'when Scripture spoke of wisdom.'
last_rejected.fix: For it was said of him when wisdom was being spoken of:
last_rejected.ruling: 'Scripture spoke of' paraphrases 'cum de sapientia diceretur'; no meaning lost, reader not misled.
